name: Pale Olive-Buff
lede: Pale Olive-Buff is a muted, light tan, the pale tone Robert Ridgway charted beside the parent color Olive-Buff in his 1912 color atlas.

sections.title: A pale tone of Olive-Buff
sections.body:
Pale Olive-Buff puts Ridgway's tone word Pale in front of [[olive-buff]], the paired-tone method his 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* used across the atlas [1]. Olive-Buff itself is Ridgway's plate XL, hue 21 triple-prime, tone d, later filed by the ISCC-NBS dictionary of 1955 in block 89 [1].

Its nearest named neighbor is [[light-ivory]], 3.4 units off and yellower than this swatch [1]; [[beige]] sits 3.6 units away, reading more vivid, and [[bone]] 4.0 units away, almost the same [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds this color in 2,438 of 23,781 paintings, 10.25 percent, as photographed; narrowing to at least five percent coverage inside a painting leaves 1,701 [2]. That makes it more common than 94 percent of the named colors in our library [2]. It peaks in the 1100s, present in 28.0 percent of the 50 paintings we have from then, 1.8 times the archive's overall rate [2]. Inside a painting it most often plays a light, in 51 percent of its 1,701 appearances by lightness rank [2].

The earliest match dates to 900, in a work attributed to Zhao Guangfu, a floor and not a first since the archive's early centuries are thin; that is 1,012 years before the name's 1912 record, so the match marks a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not a surviving pigment [2]. Willem van de Velde (I) used it most, in 9 of his 14 paintings here, 7.7 times the rate of the museums those works come from, and it is most over-represented in paintings from Iran, 2.8 times the expected rate [2].
